text.en: In a 1999 study with a synthesized choir, each singer liked their own voice at a narrow level, typically within 2 decibels either way, but levels ranged from about even to 15 decibels louder.

headline.en: Learn a choir part the way it sticks: hear it in the whole sound, then on its own, then sing it with the others.

detail.en: The start of the song, every part
Pick soprano, alto, tenor or bass: it's set in your own range, and you can change it any time
Sing at an easy, medium-soft volume, not a whisper. If a note sits too high or low, sing it lightly, never louder. Stop if anything tightens or hurts.

headline.en: Now the alto on its own. Follow the words.

detail.en: It starts low and holds, then climbs
Most of the way you sit under the tune. Lost? Find the tune and stay under it.

headline.en: Now the soprano on its own: the tune. Follow the words.

detail.en: It starts on home, dips low on "all" and again on "faithful", then leaps up and climbs to "triumphant"
You carry the tune, the line the others fit around. Lost? Come back in at the next line.

headline.en: Now the tenor on its own. Follow the words.

detail.en: It starts low and holds, climbs to "faithful", then stays on that note through most of "joyful and triumphant"
Most of the way you sit under the alto and over the bass. Lost? Find the bass and stay above it.

headline.en: Now the bass on its own. Follow the words.

detail.en: It climbs to "faithful", then jumps about on "joyful and triumphant"
You're the lowest line, often on the chord's bottom note. Lost? Listen for the chord and find its bottom note.

text.en: Find the notes of line 1: each one waits until you're on it.
Sing lines 1 and 2 with the guide and the other parts around you.

measures.en: Scored on the notes. Listen back: could you hear your line inside the chords?

headline.en: At rehearsal the pianist plays a chord, and you find your note in it.

detail.en: Hear the chord's bottom, middle and top notes, then sing the one asked for
It starts on the chord's middle note, below the tune
Hear the note in your head first, then start right on it

headline.en: At rehearsal the pianist plays a chord, and you find your note in it.

detail.en: Hear the chord's bottom, middle and top notes, then sing the one asked for
It starts on home, the bass's note sung high, at the top of the sound
Hear the note in your head first, then start right on it

headline.en: At rehearsal the pianist plays a chord, and you find your note in it.

detail.en: Hear the chord's bottom, middle and top notes, then sing the one asked for
It starts on the chord's bottom note, home, an octave under the tune
Hear the note in your head first, then start right on it

headline.en: At rehearsal the pianist plays a chord, and you find your note in it.

detail.en: Hear the chord's bottom, middle and top notes, then sing the one asked for
It starts on the chord's bottom note, home, the lowest note in the sound
Hear the note in your head first, then start right on it

text.en: Hear the chord's three notes, then sing the one asked for: the middle note, the top note, then the bottom one.
Now line 1 starting cold: no guide, the other parts on. Give me my note is there if you need it.

headline.en: In a choir score your line is one of four. Find it, follow it with the words, and see where it climbs and where it holds.

detail.en: Three notes the same, then up
At "faithful" your line ends above the tune. Hold your note.
Pencil in your score where you'll breathe, so you never run out mid-line

headline.en: In a choir score your line is one of four. Find it, follow it with the words, and see where it climbs and where it holds.

detail.en: Two notes the same, then down to "all" and back up
At "faithful" the tune falls a fifth to its lowest note, the one you sang on "all". Land it lightly.
Pencil in your score where you'll breathe, so you never run out mid-line

headline.en: In a choir score your line is one of four. Find it, follow it with the words, and see where it climbs and where it holds.

detail.en: Three notes the same, then up
At "faithful" the tune comes down to your note, so you both sing the same note. Hold it steady.
Pencil in your score where you'll breathe, so you never run out mid-line

headline.en: In a choir score your line is one of four. Find it, follow it with the words, and see where it climbs and where it holds.

detail.en: Two notes the same, up a third to two more the same, then up a step at a time
Your line climbs to "faithful": hold "faith-" its full two beats, then step up.
Pencil in your score where you'll breathe, so you never run out mid-line

text.en: Read line 1 on the stave and sing it with the guide.
Line 2, the names fainter now: read it and sing it with the guide.
Lines 1 and 2 cold: find your first note, then no guide, just you and the other parts.
In a 2009 study, advanced pianists practised a hard three-bar passage. How long they practised didn't predict how well they played it the next day. What share of their tries they played right did.

source.en: Duke, Simmons and Cash, Journal of Research in Music Education (2009)

headline.en: Learn a new line a little slower, then join it to the next, so the joins get practised too. The joins are where singers get lost.

detail.en: Hear it, then sing it back
The same
At speed, with the guide, straight through the join

text.en: Hear line 3, a little slower, then sing it back.
Hear line 4, a little slower, then sing it back.
Lines 3 and 4 joined, at speed, with the guide.

headline.en: Most of a part comes easily. A few bars don't: give them the time.

detail.en: A jump, a note from outside the key, or your line moving while the others hold
On "-hem" you slip down a half step to a note from outside the key, just above the second "O" and "to", then leap up a fourth to a long note above the tune.
Same notes, same pitch, much slower. Take a quick breath from the end of "O come ye," and keep it easy.

headline.en: Most of a part comes easily. A few bars don't: give them the time.

detail.en: A jump, a note from outside the key, or your line moving while the others hold
The line climbs a step at a time to "Beth-", then the tune drops a fourth on "-le-" and steps down to a long low note on "-hem".
Same notes, same pitch, much slower. Take a quick breath from the end of "O come ye," and keep it easy.

headline.en: Most of a part comes easily. A few bars don't: give them the time.

detail.en: A jump, a note from outside the key, or your line moving while the others hold
On "to" you dip a third to a low note, climb back on "Bethlehem", then stay on one note from "-le-" to the end, almost seven beats. Keep it steady as the chords change.
Same notes, same pitch, much slower. Take a quick breath from the end of "O come ye," and keep it easy.

headline.en: Most of a part comes easily. A few bars don't: give them the time.

detail.en: A jump, a note from outside the key, or your line moving while the others hold
The line steps up and rocks, drops a third on "to", then "Bethlehem" jumps: up a third, down a fourth, then up a fourth to a long note.
Same notes, same pitch, much slower. Take a quick breath from the end of "O come ye," and keep it easy.

text.en: Line 3, slowly: each note waits until you're on it.
Line 3 slowly on the stave, with the guide: watch for the note from outside the key.

soprano.en: Line 3 slowly on the stave, with the guide: watch for the drop on "Bethlehem".

tenor.en: Line 3 slowly on the stave, with the guide: watch the dip on "to" and the long last note.

bass.en: Line 3 slowly on the stave, with the guide: watch the drop on "to" and the jumps on "Bethlehem".

headline.en: Slow and clean first, then a little faster each time. A bar you can sing slowly comes at speed; a bar you always rush never does.

detail.en: With the guide
Still with the guide
No guide, the other parts on, as at rehearsal

text.en: Line 3 a little faster, with the guide.
Faster again, with the guide.
Full speed, the guide off, the other parts on.
The verse at full speed, the guide off: the hard bar where it lives.
In 1890 William James wrote that once you almost know a piece by heart, "it pays better to wait and recollect by an effort from within" than to look at the book again.

source.en: James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), chapter 16, York University Classics in the History of Psychology

headline.en: The three "O come, let us adore him" lines share the words and the same three neighbouring notes, in a different order each time. The first drops low on "him", the second ends high, and the third drops low again, then goes on to "Christ the Lord".

detail.en: Meanwhile the tune climbs, so you can't just follow it
Cut "him" off short, breathe in the rest, and come in on "O" just before the beat

headline.en: The three "O come, let us adore him" lines build: the second is much the same shape a third higher, and the third starts there, steps down through "adore him", then leaps up a fourth to "Christ the Lord".

detail.en: The alto and tenor stay near their notes while you rise. The climb is yours: let it grow, never push.
Cut "him" off short, breathe in the rest, and come in on "O" just before the beat

headline.en: The three "O come, let us adore him" lines are each different for you: the first leaps up a fifth on "us", to the alto's note, the second stays almost on one note, and the third stays near it, then falls to "Lord".

detail.en: In the second line the tune climbs while you stay near one note. Don't drift up with it.
Cut "him" off short, breathe in the rest, and come in on "O" just before the beat

headline.en: The three "O come, let us adore him" lines jump for you: the first drops a sixth to a low "him", the second starts an octave above it, and the third starts back on the low note.

detail.en: Before line 6, hear its first note in your head: an octave above your last "him", on the tenor's note
Cut "him" off short, breathe in the rest, and come in on "O" just before the beat

text.en: Hear line 5, a little slower, then sing it back.
Line 6 on the stave, a little slower, with the guide: spot what changed.
The whole refrain at speed, with the guide and the other parts.

headline.en: The last line jumps: up a fourth to "Christ", up a third to "Lord", then down a fifth inside "Lord" to a long low note.

detail.en: Shorten "him," a little to breathe, then sing "Christ the Lord" in one breath
With the guide, then without
Your long low note is the chord's middle note: listen for it to settle

headline.en: The last line climbs a fourth to "Christ", then steps down through "the Lord" to a long note on home.

detail.en: Shorten "him," a little to breathe, then sing "Christ the Lord" in one breath
With the guide, then without
Your long last note is the chord's bottom note, home: listen for it to settle

headline.en: The last line stays put: "him, Christ the" on one note, then down a fourth to "Lord", on the bass's note: your lowest, held long.

detail.en: Shorten "him," a little to breathe, then sing "Christ the Lord" in one breath
With the guide, then without
Hold your low note steady while the chord changes under it. It ends as the chord's top note, sung low.

headline.en: The last line moves down a third to "Christ", up a step to "the", then down a fifth inside "Lord" to a long low note.

detail.en: Shorten "him," a little to breathe, then sing "Christ the Lord" in one breath
With the guide, then without
Your long low note is the chord's bottom note, home: listen for the others to settle on it

text.en: Hear the last line slowly, then sing it back.
The last line a little faster, with the guide and the chords.
The last line at speed, the guide off, the other parts on.

headline.en: The guide is there to learn from, then to put down. Put it down early: at rehearsal there's no guide in your ear.

detail.en: Every line you've learned, joined
Halfway through your notes stop lighting: keep going by ear

text.en: The whole part with the guide and the other parts. Halfway, the lights fade.
The whole part, start to end: no guide, the other parts on. Find your first note as you did before; Give me my note is there if you need it.
In a 2006 study, people who learned a short piano melody played it more accurately after a night's sleep, with no further practice. The same hours awake brought no significant gain.

source.en: Simmons and Duke, Journal of Research in Music Education (2006)

headline.en: The night before: one run-through at full speed, then rest your voice. The morning of: a short, gentle hum, then your first note.

detail.en: Soft and easy, against a quiet drone
Found cold, as at rehearsal

text.en: Hum a soft, easy, straight "mm" on the drone's note, three times: one plain tone, no wave.

measures.en: Scored on how straight the hum stayed: no wave in it.

text.en: The refrain cold: no guide, the other parts on.

headline.en: At rehearsal nobody stops for you. If you get lost, listen, and come back in at the start of the next line.

detail.en: Your notes are shown after the take, not during it
Keep listening. The rests between lines, like the one after each "him", are your way back in.

text.en: The whole part with the other parts, no guide, nothing lit while you sing. Sing it as you will at rehearsal.

headline.en: What you've just done works for every piece: hear it, find your note, a line at a time, fix the hard bars, put the guide down, and don't stop.

detail.en: Every library song has Learn it step by step, part by part: pick yours
The whole part in Sing, with the other three parts
If your director uses Stackapella, a choir group puts the choir's songs in one place, with your part already picked.

text.en: First, the two lines you began with, now on your own. Then hear how far you've come.
The dress rehearsal: record your part in Sing, with the other three parts around you.

measures.en: Scored on the notes of your recording.
